narrative: The model estimated a 63% chance that you would fail the bar exam on the first attempt. In practical terms, it judged failure more likely than passing, and that risk estimate is why your law school application was denied. The strongest factor was your year-three academic standing: you were in the first decile, while admitted students averaged around the sixth decile, and this much lower relative standing pushed the prediction most strongly toward failure. Your year-one standing was the second most influential factor; it was also first-decile versus an admitted-student average near the sixth decile, and it also pushed toward failure. Your LSAT score of 30.5, below the admitted-student average of about 37.2, was the third most influential factor, but in your case it worked slightly in the opposite direction—toward passing—so it was not the reason for denial. Your undergraduate GPA was close to the admitted average, and gender and race were not used. To move forward, ask admissions for a feedback meeting, focus on strengthening your academic record and bar-readiness, consider retaking the LSAT if you can raise it, and reapply only after showing concrete improvement. A written explanation of any academic difficulties and a realistic study plan would also help.
